metadata.title: Immigration status and adolescents’ voting intention in European countries: The importance of immigrant integration policy context

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2009 microdata with a cluster sampling design (schools randomly selected, one Grade-8 class per school, and all students in the selected class assessed). For the within-country step, the authors explicitly state that they used the student-level weights TOTWGTS from the ICCS dataset to obtain unbiased estimates in the two-level (students nested in schools) models. The between-country step then meta-analyzes the country-specific immigrant/native voting-intention contrasts using HLM, weighting countries by the precision of their contrast estimates (inverse-variance weighting based on sampling variances Vk). The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty is handled through the HLM framework and standard errors rather than replicate-based variance estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable (Voting Intention) is described as an ICCS 2009 IRT-constructed scale standardized to mean 50 and SD 10, rather than a PV-based cognitive achievement outcome. As a result, plausible values are not the intended mechanism for uncertainty in this analysis, and PV handling is not applicable to the reported modeling. The paper also does not describe a specific missing-data strategy for individual-level covariates or the voting-intention scale; instead, it reports an overall missing category in Table 1 and discusses exclusions at the ICCS sampling frame level, which is not a complete imputation/deletion protocol for the analytic variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses use ICCS 2009 Grade-8 student data from 17 European countries (Austria, Belgium (Flemish), Cyprus, Denmark, England, Estonia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Latvia, Norway, Spain, Slovenia, Sweden, Switzerland). The authors exclude countries where the share of adolescents of immigrant origin is less than 4% of the country sample, and they also exclude the Netherlands because it did not meet ICCS sampling requirements. They further note that ICCS itself excludes some school types (e.g., specialized education schools in Belgium and Latvia) and within-sample groups (e.g., students with disabilities or language barriers), and they report an overall exclusion rate of 3.1% across the 17 countries. Within the analytic models, the paper does not specify an additional missing-data rule (e.g., listwise deletion vs imputation) for individual covariates; Table 1 reports a 'Missing' category for immigration status.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2009 Grade 8 Voting Intention (Voting Intention scale, IRT; standardized mean 50 SD 10)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM meta-analysis (between-country step): average first-generation/native contrast intercept M1 = -1.860 (SE = 0.465). Policy coefficients (Models 2–5): Political participation = 0.029 (SE = 0.021, n.s.); Education = 0.068 (SE = 0.025, p < .05); Citizenship acquisition = 0.044 (SE = 0.023, n.s.); Anti-discrimination = 0.050 (SE = 0.027, n.s.). Between-country variance (τ) and variance explained: Education model M3 τ = 1.020 (p < .05), explaining 51.3% of between-country variance; Political participation explains 16.5% (τ = 1.751, p < .01); Citizenship acquisition explains 25.8% (τ = 1.556, p < .01); Anti-discrimination explains 25.3% (τ = 1.567, p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2009 Grade 8 Voting Intention the study leveraged MIPEX integration-policy dimensions (especially education policy) to model the first-generation/native voting-intention contrast across 17 European countries, finding that more inclusive education policy significantly reduced the voting-intention gap (education coefficient 0.068, SE 0.025, p < .05; 51.3% of between-country variance explained). This indicates that strengthening immigrant-inclusive education policy may narrow first-generation immigrant–native differences in adolescents’ intended future electoral participation, though the design is correlational and does not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2009 Grade 8 Voting Intention (Voting Intention scale, IRT; standardized mean 50 SD 10)
main_findings.performance_metrics: HLM meta-analysis (between-country step): average second-generation/native contrast intercept M1 = -0.884 (SE = 0.359). Policy coefficients (Models 2–5): Political participation = 0.018 (SE = 0.016, n.s.); Education = 0.037 (SE = 0.020, n.s.); Citizenship acquisition = 0.034 (SE = 0.015, p < .05); Anti-discrimination = 0.034 (SE = 0.016, n.s.). Between-country variance (τ) and variance explained: Citizenship acquisition model M3 τ = 0.550 (n.s.), with variance explained reported as 50.4% (compared to Model 1 τ = 1.109, p < .01); Political participation explains 10.7% (τ = 0.991, p < .01); Education explains 28.5% (τ = 0.793, p < .05); Anti-discrimination explains 37.5% (τ = 0.694, p < .05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2009 Grade 8 Voting Intention the study leveraged MIPEX integration-policy dimensions to model the second-generation/native voting-intention contrast across 17 European countries, finding that citizenship acquisition policy inclusiveness was the only statistically significant predictor (citizenship acquisition coefficient 0.034, SE 0.015, p < .05) and that it substantially reduced between-country heterogeneity (reported 50.4% variance explained). This indicates that making pathways to citizenship more inclusive may help second-generation adolescents envision themselves as future voters, though the evidence remains observational and cannot confirm causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICCS 2009 Grade-8 Voting Intention (an IRT-based scale standardized to mean 50, SD 10) for 17 European countries, comparing voting-intention contrasts between first-generation and native adolescents and between second-generation and native adolescents. Using a two-step multilevel meta-analytic approach (within-country two-level models with students nested in schools, then between-country HLM models), the authors estimate country-specific immigrant/native contrasts and relate their cross-national variation to MIPEX 2010 integration-policy dimensions. For first-generation contrasts, the education-policy dimension is the key predictor (education coefficient 0.068, SE 0.025, p < .05), explaining 51.3% of between-country variance in contrasts. For second-generation contrasts, citizenship-acquisition policy is the key predictor (0.034, SE 0.015, p < .05), with large reported variance explained (50.4%). The paper does not use machine learning algorithms and does not report a missing-data imputation/deletion protocol for individual covariates, so results should be interpreted as correlational rather than causal.
